analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income, corporate, and estate taxes with a flat tax on wages and business income.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have ended all federal tax on investment income, inheritances, and the Earned Income Tax Credit, died in committee with 3 cosponsors and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have scrapped the entire federal income tax code and replaced it with a single 19% rate (dropping to 17% after 2004) on wages and business profits, with a large standard deduction shielding low-wage income. It would have repealed the estate and gift tax, the alternative minimum tax, and every individual tax credit, including the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit. Notably, it would only tax wages, retirement payouts, and unemployment benefits at the individual level — meaning money earned from capital gains, dividends, and interest would owe no federal income tax at all. It also would have stripped rules requiring retirement plans to cover lower-paid workers, and let employers pull surplus pension money back out of plans.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households living on investment income would owe no federal income tax, since the bill taxes only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation. Very large estates would pay no estate or gift tax. Businesses would pay a flat 19% on profits with immediate write-offs for equipment and inputs. Modest-wage workers would benefit from a large standard deduction ($25,580 for a married couple in 2003), but would lose the credits that currently cut or eliminate their taxes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: It replaces the graduated income tax rates with a single 19% rate on individuals, dropping to 17% after 2004.
It taxes only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation at the individual level, so capital gains, dividends, and interest would no longer be taxed.

It shields wages up to a large standard deduction — $25,580 for a married couple, $12,790 for a single filer in 2003, adjusted for inflation — plus $5,510 per dependent, so many low-wage workers would owe nothing.
It replaces the corporate income tax with a flat 19% tax on all business activity, letting businesses deduct the full cost of equipment, supplies, and other inputs.
It repeals the estate and gift tax for decedents dying after December 31, 2002, and repeals the alternative minimum tax.
It simplifies retirement plans by repealing nondiscrimination, coverage, and contribution-limit rules, and removes the penalty on early retirement withdrawals.

analysis.who_pays: Working families who rely on the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit would see those disappear. Wage earners generally would bear more of the federal tax burden as investment income and inheritances went untaxed and major revenue sources were repealed. Workers' retirement security would be weaker: plans could favor highly paid employees and employers could reclaim excess pension assets. Employer-paid benefits like health insurance would effectively cost more, since businesses could no longer deduct them and tax-exempt employers and governments would owe a 19% tax on their value.
analysis.who_pays_short: Working families and the federal Treasury

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals all individual tax credits — including the Earned Income Tax Credit and the Child Tax Credit — which currently reduce or wipe out taxes for millions of low- and middle-income working families.

Because taxable income is defined to include only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, income from capital gains, dividends, and interest — concentrated among the wealthiest households — would owe no federal income tax, shifting the burden onto paychecks.

Repealing the estate and gift tax, the alternative minimum tax, and taxation of investment income while cutting rates would eliminate major federal revenue sources, leaving a large hole funded by deficits or spending cuts.

Employers would no longer deduct the cost of fringe benefits such as health insurance, and tax-exempt organizations and governments would owe a 19% tax on the value of such benefits — raising the cost of employer-provided health coverage.

It repeals the rules that require retirement plans to cover lower-paid workers and not favor executives, and lets employers take excess pension assets back out of plans without the current excise tax.

Title II would make it out of order for Congress to consider any bill that raises income tax rates or reduces federal revenues unless three-fifths of each chamber votes to waive the rule — an attempt to lock in the tax cut against future Congresses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplification is real: a flat tax with no deductions, credits, or AMT would make filing dramatically easier, and the large standard deduction would take many low-wage workers off the tax rolls entirely. But the design pairs those gains with a sweeping transfer away from taxed capital: investment income, inheritances, and large estates would owe nothing, while credits that lift working families out of poverty would vanish. The bill would also strip protections that keep retirement plans from favoring executives, and its Title II rule would handcuff future Congresses from reversing the revenue loss. Weighed honestly, the gains flow disproportionately to the top of the income distribution, and the costs fall on wage earners and on whoever has to fill the revenue gap.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Nick Smith of Michigan introduced the bill on September 10, 2003, with three cosponsors — two Republicans and one Democrat.
The same day, it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and, for portions within its jurisdiction, the Rules Committee.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it received no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing tax structure survived intact: working families who claim the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit kept those benefits, retirement plans kept their nondiscrimination and coverage rules, and the Treasury kept the revenue from the estate tax and investment income taxation that the bill would have repealed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working families who claim tax credits

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill, so the record shows only sponsorship — three Republicans and one Democrat — with no recorded floor opposition.

industries.note: Under the bill's definition of taxable income, capital gains, dividends, and interest would owe no federal income tax, and the estate and gift tax would be repealed. The resulting revenue gap and the flat tax on wages would shift the tax burden onto paychecks.

The bill repeals the rules requiring plans to cover lower-paid workers and limit benefits for executives, removes contribution limits, and lets employers pull excess pension assets back out of plans without the current excise tax. Workers' retirement protections are the offsetting loss.

industries.industry: Employers providing health and fringe benefits
industries.note: Businesses could no longer deduct the cost of fringe benefits such as health insurance, and tax-exempt employers and governments would owe a 19% tax on their value. The cost would likely be passed on through reduced or pricier benefits for workers.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: A flat tax with no itemized deductions, credits, or AMT would sharply shrink the compliance work that individual and business filers currently pay for. Ordinary filers would share the same benefit of simpler taxes.
